noteBlocks.lede: A tin of beans, an ice-cream cone and a football. Volume is how much each one holds; surface area is the skin you would have to cut to make it. Half the formulae are printed for you, and the work is deciding which of the two a question is actually asking for.
can: Halve a diameter before it enters any formula.
Choose between volume and surface area from what the question is about.
Tell a cone's perpendicular height from its slant height, and link them by Pythagoras.

noteBlocks.md: Four solids, eight formulae, and **half of them are printed for you**. The trouble is never the arithmetic: it is choosing between volume and surface area, and between the two heights of a cone. Volume is what a shape holds — litres, capacity, melting and recasting. Surface area is its skin — labels, paint, the metal sheet a tin is cut from. Decide which one the question wants before you reach for a formula.

Volume of a cylinder

noteBlocks.text: What is given and what is memory

noteBlocks.title: The split
noteBlocks.md:
**Given on the sheet:** $\tfrac{1}{3}\pi r^2 h$ (cone volume), $\pi r l$ (cone curved surface), $\tfrac{4}{3}\pi r^3$ (sphere volume), $4\pi r^2$ (sphere surface), volume of a prism.
**Memory:** $\pi r^2 h$ and $2\pi r h$ for the cylinder, $\pi r^2$ and $2\pi r$ for the circle, the hemisphere as half a sphere, $\pi r l + \pi r^2$ for a cone's total surface, and $1$ litre $= 1000$ cm³.

noteBlocks.prompt: Write the curved surface area of a cylinder of radius $r$ and height $h$.
noteBlocks.explain: Yes. It is the unrolled rectangle: circumference times height. Adding the two circles as well would give the total surface area.

noteBlocks.md:
Decide this first, before any formula. Ask what the question is really about:

**Volume** — how much it holds or how much material it is made of. Litres, capacity, melting and recasting, filling cups. Units are cubic: cm³.
**Surface area** — the skin. Labels, paint, wrapping, the metal sheet a tin is cut from. Units are square: cm².

The unit at the end is the check. If your answer is in cm³ and the question wanted a label, something went wrong at the first step, not the last.

noteBlocks.prompt: A label is wrapped round a tin, covering the curved surface only. What are you finding?
noteBlocks.explain: Yes. A label is a surface, so it is 2πrh, and the answer is in square centimetres.
options: An area, in cm²
A volume, in cm³
A length, in cm

noteBlocks.md:
The **perpendicular height** $h$ runs straight up the middle to the point. The **slant height** $l$ runs up the sloping edge. They are different numbers, and each formula wants a particular one.

**Volume** $= \tfrac{1}{3}\pi r^2 h$ uses $h$.
**Curved surface** $= \pi r l$ uses $l$.

If the question gives one and you need the other, Pythagoras links them: $l^2 = r^2 + h^2$, because the radius, the height and the slant make a right-angled triangle inside the cone.

noteBlocks.caption: With $r = 5$ and $h = 12$: $l^2 = 5^2 + 12^2 = 169$, so $l = 13$ cm.

noteBlocks.prompt: A cone has radius 5 cm and perpendicular height 12 cm. What is its slant height, in cm?
noteBlocks.explain: Yes: $5^2 + 12^2 = 169$ and the square root of that is 13.

noteBlocks.title: Volume of a Cone
noteBlocks.why: Three minutes on substituting into the cone formula. Notice that the height used is always the one drawn as a dashed line inside the cone.

noteBlocks.prompt: Which height does the volume formula use?
noteBlocks.explain: Yes. The slant height belongs to πrl only. Using the slant height in the volume makes the answer too big.
options: The perpendicular height
The slant height
Either one

noteBlocks.text: Hemispheres: halve, then look for the flat face

noteBlocks.md:
A hemisphere is half a sphere, so its **volume** is $\tfrac{1}{2} \times \tfrac{4}{3}\pi r^3 = \tfrac{2}{3}\pi r^3$ and its **curved surface** is $\tfrac{1}{2} \times 4\pi r^2 = 2\pi r^2$.

Surface area needs one more thought. Cutting the sphere in half made a **new flat circle**, so a solid hemisphere's total surface is $2\pi r^2 + \pi r^2 = 3\pi r^2$. A bowl, open at the top, has only the curved part.

noteBlocks.alt: A hemisphere with its flat circular face uppermost and its radius labelled.
noteBlocks.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 300 250' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg' role='img' aria-labelledby='sl26'><title id='sl26'>A hemisphere with its flat circular face and radius labelled</title><g fill='none' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='1.7'><path d='M58,118 A92,92 0 0 0 242,118 Z'/></g><g fill='none' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='1.4'><ellipse cx='150' cy='118' rx='92' ry='20'/></g><g fill='none' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='1.1'><path d='M150,118 H242'/></g><g fill='currentColor' font-family='inherit' font-size='13'><text x='196' y='110' text-anchor='middle'>r</text><text x='150' y='240' text-anchor='middle'>flat circular face on top</text></g><g fill='currentColor' font-family='inherit' font-size='11'><text x='6' y='16'>diagram not drawn</text><text x='6' y='29'>accurately</text></g></svg>
noteBlocks.caption: Half a sphere, plus the circle the cut created. Whether that circle counts depends on whether the solid is closed.

noteBlocks.prompt: Write the volume of a hemisphere of radius $r$ as a single fraction times $\pi r^3$.
noteBlocks.explain: Yes: half of 4/3 is 2/3, so the volume is (2/3)πr³.

noteBlocks.title: Summer 2024, M3 Q24 and M4 Q9
noteBlocks.md:
A cylinder of coffee was poured into hemispherical cups filled to **90%**. Three separate losses ran through the scripts: the sphere formula left unhalved, the 90% ignored, and a decimal left as the number of cups.
All three are habits rather than knowledge: halve, apply the percentage, round the count **down**.

noteBlocks.prompt: A jug holds 1500 cm³. Each cup holds 180 cm³. How many cups can be filled completely?
noteBlocks.explain: Yes: 1500 ÷ 180 = 8.33, and the ninth cup would not be full, so the answer is 8.

noteBlocks.text: Units, litres and the answer line

noteBlocks.md:
$1$ litre $= 1000$ cm³, and that is the conversion the specification expects you to know. Divide by $1000$ to go from cm³ to litres.

Keep the full calculator display through every step and round **once**, on the answer line, to the accuracy the question names. If a question says 3 significant figures, give exactly that.

noteBlocks.title: Why a cone is a third of its cylinder
noteBlocks.md: Stand a cone inside a cylinder of the same radius and height and it fills exactly one third of the room. Its horizontal slices are circles that shrink to nothing at the tip, and those shrinking circles add up to a third of the full stack. That is where the $\tfrac{1}{3}$ comes from.

noteBlocks.answer: The cone is one third of the cylinder

options: The cone is one third of the cylinder
The cone is half of the cylinder
They are equal

noteBlocks.md:
Decide between volume and surface area before any formula.
Halve a diameter, and keep a cone's two heights apart.
Halve a sphere for a hemisphere, and add the flat circle when it is closed.

A single solid is worth about three marks; a capacity problem with a percentage and a count is worth five. The first mark is the right formula with the right numbers in it, named beside the working. The last is the rounded value with its unit, and the count rounded down where the context demands it. Stuck: write the formula you would use and substitute — a named substitution scores on its own.

options: Because πr²h squares the radius, so doubling it multiplies the volume by four
Because the diameter is always odd
Because the height must be halved too
whyMenu.explain: Using 14 in place of 7 would give 13547 cm³ instead of 3387 cm³: four times too big, because the radius is squared.

steps.decision: The cone volume is on the Higher sheet. It uses the perpendicular height, the dashed line straight up the middle, never the sloping edge.

The curved surface formula needs the slant height, and only the radius and the perpendicular height were given. The radius, the height and the slant make a right-angled triangle, so Pythagoras supplies it.

options: Because the radius, the height and the slant height form a right-angled triangle
Because the slant height is always the radius plus the height
Because πrl needs the height
whyMenu.explain: Adding would give 17 cm, which is longer than the true slant of 13 cm. The right angle is at the centre of the base, so squares are what add.

steps.decision: This one is on the sheet as $\pi r l$. Total surface area is asked for, so this is not the end.

steps.decision: Melting changes the shape, not the amount of metal, so the two volumes are equal. The sphere formula is on the Higher sheet.

options: Because melting and recasting keeps the volume the same
Because the radius stays the same
Because a sphere and a cylinder always have equal volumes
whyMenu.explain: The metal is conserved. That single sentence is what turns this into an equation you can solve.

steps.decision: Write the equation before rearranging. The unknown is the height, and the cylinder formula is the one you must know.
Divide by everything that multiplies $h$. The answer is exactly 9 cm, which is a sign the numbers were chosen to work out: $\tfrac{4}{3}\pi(3)^3 = 36\pi$ and $\pi(2)^2 = 4\pi$.

items.stem: A question asks for the total surface area of a solid cone. You have worked out πrl. What is still missing?

items.stem: A container holds 4500 cm³. How many litres is that?
items.skill: Convert between cubic centimetres and litres

options.feedback: Yes: 1 litre = 1000 cm³, so divide by 1000.
That divides by 100. A litre is 1000 cm³ — the volume of a 10 cm cube.
That divides by 10 000. Dividing by 1000 gives 4.5.
Multiplying by 1000 makes it bigger; changing to a larger unit makes the number smaller.

items.stem: A jug holds 1500 cm³ of juice. Each glass holds 180 cm³. How many full glasses can be poured?
items.skill: Round a count down, whatever the decimal says

options.feedback: Yes: 1500 ÷ 180 = 8.33, and the ninth glass would not be full, so 8.
8.33 rounds up to 9 by the usual rule, but there is not enough juice for a ninth full glass. Counts like this are rounded down.
A number of glasses has to be a whole number. The Summer 2024 report noted that a decimal answer lost the final mark.
That is the division, not the answer to the question asked. Finish by deciding how many glasses are full.

items.stem: A cylinder of volume 600 cm³ has radius 5 cm. How do you find its height?
items.skill: Work backwards from a given volume

options.feedback: Yes. π(5)² is the area of the cross-section, and volume ÷ cross-section = length.

options.text: Work out π(5)² and stop there
options.feedback: That is the cross-section area, a useful step but not the height. Summer 2024 M3 Q17 lost marks at exactly this point.
The radius is squared in the cylinder formula, so the divisor is π(5)², not π(5).
Multiplying makes the answer larger than the volume itself. To undo a multiplication, divide.

parts.stem:
A water butt is a cylinder of radius 30 cm and height 90 cm.

Calculate the volume of the water butt. Give your answer to the nearest cubic centimetre.
hints: A cylinder is a prism with a circular cross-section.
Volume = area of the circle × height.
parts.workedSolution: $V = \pi(30)^2(90) = 254469.0049$ cm³, so $254469$ cm³ to the nearest cubic centimetre.

commonErrors.feedback: That is the curved surface area in cm². A capacity is a volume, so multiply the circle's area by the height.
That is the area of the base circle. One more step, multiplying by the height, finishes it.

parts.stem:
The water butt is filled to 85% of its capacity.

Calculate the volume of water in the butt, in litres. Give your answer to 1 decimal place.

scheme.for: divides by 1000 to change cm³ to litres

hints: Take 85% of the volume from part (a).
Then change cubic centimetres to litres.

commonErrors.feedback: That is the full capacity in litres. The butt is only 85% full, so multiply by 0.85 first.
The percentage is right, so the first mark stands. Dividing by 100 gives centilitres; a litre is 1000 cm³.

parts.stem:
A solid cone has base radius 9 cm and perpendicular height 12 cm.

Calculate the slant height $l$ of the cone.
hints: The radius, the height and the slant height make a right-angled triangle.
Pythagoras: square, add, square-root.

commonErrors.feedback: The radius and the height have been added. They meet at a right angle, so it is their squares that add.
That subtracts the squares, which is the move for finding a shorter side. Here the slant height is the longest side, so the squares are added.

parts.stem: Calculate the total surface area of the cone. Give your answer to 1 decimal place.
hints: πrl is given on the formula sheet and uses the slant height.
A solid cone also has a base.
parts.workedSolution: Curved surface $= \pi(9)(15) = 424.1150$ cm². Base $= \pi(9)^2 = 254.4690$ cm². Total $= 678.5840$ cm², so $678.6$ cm².

commonErrors.feedback: The curved surface is right, so that mark stands. The word total means the base circle counts as well.
The perpendicular height has gone into πrl. That formula needs the slant height from part (a).
That is a volume in cubic centimetres. The question asks for the surface area.

parts.stem:
A carton holds 2 litres of juice.

A glass is a hemisphere of diameter 8 cm. Each glass is filled to 80% of its capacity.

Work out how many glasses can be filled from one carton.
hints: Work in the same units: change litres to cubic centimetres.
The glass is a hemisphere, so halve the sphere formula, and it is only filled to 80%.
A part-filled glass does not count.
parts.workedSolution: $2$ litres $= 2000$ cm³. Glass $= \tfrac{1}{2} \times \tfrac{4}{3}\pi(4)^3 = 134.0413$ cm³, and 80% of that is $107.2330$ cm³. Number of glasses $= 2000 \div 107.2330 = 18.6510$, so $18$ glasses can be filled.

commonErrors.feedback: The whole sphere formula was used for the glass, so each one looks twice as big. Halve it: a hemisphere is half a sphere.
The 80% has been left out, so each glass is treated as full to the brim. Multiply the glass volume by 0.80 first.
All the method is right, so four marks stand. There is not enough juice for glass number 19, so round the count down.

figures.alt: A cylinder of radius 3 cm and height 10 cm.

parts.stem:
A solid metal cylinder has radius 3 cm and height 10 cm.

Find its volume. Leave your answer in terms of $\pi$.
hints: πr²h, with π left alone.

commonErrors.feedback: That is the area of the circular end, 9π cm². Multiplying by the height gives the volume.
That is the curved surface area, 60π cm². The volume squares the radius.

parts.stem:
The cylinder is melted down and made into solid spheres of radius 1 cm.

Work out how many complete spheres can be made.
hints: Divide the cylinder's volume by one sphere's volume.
The πs cancel, which is why the exact form was worth keeping.
A part sphere is not a complete sphere.
parts.workedSolution: One sphere $= \tfrac{4}{3}\pi(1)^3 = \tfrac{4}{3}\pi$ cm³. Number $= 90\pi \div \tfrac{4}{3}\pi = 90 \times \tfrac{3}{4} = 67.5$, so $67$ complete spheres can be made.

commonErrors.feedback: The division is right, so two marks stand. Half a sphere is not a complete sphere, so the count rounds down to 67.
The sphere's radius is 1 cm, not its diameter. Using 2 cm makes each sphere eight times too big, so far too few come out.

findTheMistake.stem: A label wraps right round the curved surface of a tin of radius 4 cm and height 15 cm, with a 2 cm overlap so it can be stuck down. Seán was asked for the area of the label. His working:
findTheMistake.whatWentWrong: The curved surface is right and earns its mark. The 2 cm overlap is a length, and a length cannot be added to an area. The label is a rectangle whose width is the circumference plus the overlap, 25.1327 + 2 = 27.1327 cm, and whose height is 15 cm.
findTheMistake.feedback: One mark stands for the curved surface. The check that catches this every time is the unit: cm² can only be added to cm². Summer 2023 asked this on both M3 Q24 and M4 Q13, and very few candidates were fully correct; the ones who were treated the overlap as a 2 cm by 15 cm strip.

findTheMistake.stem: A jug holds 1800 cm³ of soup. A bowl is a hemisphere of diameter 9 cm and is filled to 90% of its capacity. Méabh was asked how many bowls can be filled. Her working:
findTheMistake.whatWentWrong: The radius is right, the percentage is applied properly and the final division is set up correctly, so most of the method stands. Line 2 uses the whole sphere. A bowl shaped like a hemisphere holds half that, 190.8518 cm³.
findTheMistake.feedback: Three marks stand: the radius, the percentage and the division are all right. Write the word hemisphere beside the formula and the halving becomes hard to forget. The Summer 2024 reports on M3 Q24 and M4 Q9 named this, together with the ignored percentage, as the reason so few reached the right count.

findTheMistake.stem: Dáire was asked for the total surface area of a solid cylinder of radius 6 cm and height 20 cm. His working:
findTheMistake.whatWentWrong: The question asks for surface area, the skin of the solid, but the volume formula has been used, which measures the space inside. Nothing after line 1 can recover the marks, because the wrong quantity is being calculated.
findTheMistake.feedback: No marks here, and the cost is only one habit away from being avoided: underline the words total surface area in the question, then write the list of faces before any formula. Summer 2025 M3 Q19 and Summer 2023 M3 Q24 both turned on this, and the units are the tell — an area answer must be in cm².

prompts.prompt: Which solid formulae are printed on the CCEA Higher formula sheet?
prompts.answer: Volume of a cone (1/3)πr²h, curved surface area of a cone πrl, volume of a sphere (4/3)πr³, surface area of a sphere 4πr², volume of a prism and area of a trapezium. Nothing for the cylinder.

prompts.prompt: Give the volume and the total surface area of a cylinder.
prompts.answer: V = πr²h and S = 2πrh + 2πr². Neither is on the formula sheet.

prompts.prompt: Give the volume and the curved surface area of a hemisphere of radius r.
prompts.answer: Volume = (2/3)πr³ (half the sphere) and curved surface = 2πr². A solid hemisphere also has a flat circle of πr².

prompts.prompt: A cone's volume and its curved surface area need different lengths. Which is which?
prompts.answer: Volume uses the perpendicular height h; πrl uses the slant height l. They are linked by l² = r² + h².

prompts.prompt: A question asks for the total surface area of a solid cone. What do you add to πrl?
prompts.answer: The base circle, πr². The formula sheet gives the curved surface only.

prompts.prompt: How many cubic centimetres are in a litre?
prompts.answer: 1000 cm³, the volume of a cube of side 10 cm. To change cm³ to litres, divide by 1000.

prompts.prompt: You divide a container's volume by a cup's volume and get 16.4. How many full cups?
prompts.answer: 16. A count of full cups is rounded down, whatever the usual rounding rule would say.

prompts.prompt: A cylinder's volume and radius are given. How do you find the height?
prompts.answer: Divide the volume by the area of the circular cross-section: h = V ÷ πr².

prompts.prompt: A question gives you a volume. What does that usually mean?
prompts.answer: That the volume is the start of the working, not the finish: you are being asked for something you have not found yet, such as a height, a radius or a number of containers.

prompts.prompt: A sphere of radius 3 cm is melted and recast as a cylinder of radius 2 cm. What is the cylinder's height?
prompts.answer: 9 cm. The sphere is 36π cm³, the cylinder's cross-section is 4π cm², and 36π ÷ 4π = 9.

prompts.prompt: What does curved surface area mean for a cylinder, and what does total surface area add?
prompts.answer: Curved surface area is the tube alone, 2πrh, the rectangle you get by unrolling it. Total surface area adds the two circular ends, 2πr².

findings.asked: Curved surface area of a cylindrical label with a 1 cm overlap.
findings.wentWrong: Few finished. The usual attempt found the curved surface (2 pi r h) and then added 1 to the area; others added the centimetre to the radius or diameter, or added the two circular ends.
findings.fullMarkAnswersDid: Treated the overlap as a 1 cm by 12 cm rectangle, or added 1 cm to the circumference before multiplying by the height.
findings.rule: An overlap is extra length around the label - it becomes an area only when multiplied by the height.

findings.asked: The same label problem on M3.
findings.wentWrong: The vast majority reached for the volume formula.
findings.rule: A label is a surface: use area formulas.

findings.asked: Apex angle of the sector that folds into a given cone.
findings.wentWrong: Most got the height from the volume and the slant height by Pythagoras; a few found the curved surface or the base circumference, but almost nobody linked that to the sector.
findings.fullMarkAnswersDid: Set the arc length of the sector (radius = slant height) equal to the circumference of the cone's base and solved for the angle.
findings.rule: Sector arc = base circumference; sector radius = slant height.

findings.asked: Cups from a cylinder and a hemisphere filled to 90%.
findings.wentWrong: The cylinder volume was fine; the hemisphere was left as a full sphere or the 90% was ignored; a non-integer count lost the last mark.
findings.rule: Halve the sphere, apply the percentage, round the count down.

findings.asked: The same cylinder-and-hemisphere problem on M3.
findings.wentWrong: Some quoted the curved surface area instead of the volume; the sphere was not halved; the 90% was missed; only the best divided to get 16 cups.
findings.rule: Name each solid and the formula you are using.

findings.asked: Prove the surface areas of a sphere and a cube of related dimensions can never be equal.
findings.wentWrong: Seven per cent got both marks. After writing both formulas, most substituted a number for r and lost the general argument; very few divided by r squared to compare constants.
findings.rule: A 'never' proof stays in letters - compare the coefficients.

findings.asked: Use a given volume and the container's dimensions.
findings.wentWrong: Three quarters computed the container's volume and stopped, never using the given volume.
findings.rule: If a volume is given, the question is about the volume you have not yet found.

findings.asked: Length of a trapezium-faced prism from its volume.
findings.wentWrong: Order-of-operations errors in the trapezium formula; some stopped at the cross-section area (36) thinking they were done; only the best divided the volume by it.

insight.ruleToRemember: Name each part (curved surface, ends, hemisphere = half sphere) and its formula; radius is half the diameter; label every calculation; keep the full display until the final answer, and round counts down.
insight.aStarSignal: The cone-to-sector link (arc = base circumference) and general proofs that stay in letters.
